title: How to Compare Your Website's Performance Across Countries in Google Search Console
content:
Suppose your online store sells in Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Kuwait. Your orders tell you where your customers buy, but not how your site appears in Google Search in each country: in which country your results show up most, where they get clicked most, and where your performance has improved or declined in recent months. That's information you need when deciding where to focus your next content effort or promotion.

You'll find this information in Google Search Console, the free tool that shows how your site appears in Google Search results. Keep in mind from the start that its numbers measure visibility in search and clicks on your results; they don't measure customers, sales or orders. For those, you need your analytics tool or your store dashboard.

In this article, we explain how to analyze your site's performance in different countries using Google Search Console, from viewing each country's data and comparing it with other countries to understanding the results and using them to spot opportunities to improve your site's visibility in search engines.

How Do You See Your Site's Performance in Each Country?

Open Search Console, then open the “Performance” report for Google Search results. By default, the report shows data for the last three months, with a chart at the top and a table below it with several tabs, including “Queries,” “Pages” and “Countries.” Click the “Countries” tab to see a row for every country where searches showed your site.

The report measures your site's performance with four metrics shown in boxes above the chart, and by default it displays “Total clicks” and “Total impressions.” To show the other two, “Average CTR” and “Average position,” click each of their boxes. In the Arabic interface, the last box is labeled «متوسط موضع الإعلان» (“average ad position”), but it measures the position of your regular search results, not ads:

  • “Impressions”: The number of times your site appeared in search results. It's a count of times, not people; your site may appear to the same person in more than one search.
  • “Clicks”: The number of times your site's results were clicked in Google Search. It isn't the number of unique visitors, nor the number of people who bought.
  • “CTR” (click-through rate): Clicks divided by impressions.
  • “Average position”: The average ranking of your site's topmost result on the results page. The lower the number, the higher your result.

In this report, the country is the country the search came from, not the searcher's nationality or shipping address. So if a Saudi customer searches for your store while in Cairo, that search is counted for Egypt.

If each country has its own site on a separate domain, for example a store with one site ending in .sa and another ending in .ae (an illustrative example), each has its own report, and you apply the following steps to each one separately. If your countries are folders on a single site, make sure the property you've opened in Search Console is your whole site, not a single country's folder URL, because a property added as a folder URL only shows data for that folder.

The labels in quotation marks in this guide follow the English Search Console interface and Google's help pages, and may differ slightly from what your interface shows.

How Do You Combine Several Countries in One View?

If you sell in three countries, you'll want to see their performance together, without the searches coming from countries where you don't sell. That's what Search Console has offered since October 2026: you select several countries, and their numbers are combined as if they were a single market.

  1. Click “+ Add filter” at the top of the report and choose Country.
  2. In the “Country” window, stay on the “Filter” tab, where the countries are listed with a checkbox next to each one.
  3. Select the countries you sell in, such as Saudi Arabia, the UAE and Kuwait, then click “Apply.”
  4. Check the filter bar at the top of the report: the country filter should appear there.

The numbers above the chart now show the combined total for these countries.

If the filter window doesn't offer a way to select more than one country, go back to the “Countries” tab without a filter and track your countries from their rows.

This view combines countries; it doesn't compare them. If you want to see one country against another, use the comparison.

How Do You Compare Two Countries?

A comparison puts two countries side by side, so each row in the table shows both countries' numbers and the difference between them:

  1. Open the country filter if it's already added, or add it via “+ Add filter.”
  2. In the filter window, choose “Compare.”
  3. Select the two countries, such as Saudi Arabia and the UAE.
  4. Click “Apply.”

After applying it, open the “Queries” or “Pages” tab to see the same queries and pages in both countries side by side.

Keep in mind that the report allows only one comparison at a time, as Google's help pages state. So if you already have a comparison between two date ranges and then add a comparison between two countries, the second replaces the first. You may also see the symbol ~ instead of a number in some rows, which means the value is too rare in one of the two countries for the report to show it.

How Do You Read the Comparison Results? A Practical Example

Suppose you run a certified translation office with clients in Egypt and Saudi Arabia (an illustrative example). You compare the two countries and find that your site appears more often in Egypt, but its CTR there is lower than in Saudi Arabia. What should you do?

Don't immediately conclude that your page titles don't suit the Egyptian audience. Open the “Queries” tab and look at the queries your site appears for in each country. You may find that in Egypt your site appears for broad queries unrelated to your service, and that its result gets fewer clicks for those queries because people searching them don't find what they're looking for.

Read the rest of the numbers the same way:

  • If impressions are much higher in one country, your site appears in more searches there, which doesn't necessarily mean more people.
  • If CTR differs, remember that it's affected by the queries your site appears for, what searchers want from them, your result's ranking, and what appears around it on the results page. Compare the same queries in both countries before drawing conclusions.
  • If your ranking is lower in one country, competition for the same queries may be stronger there, or people there may search using different phrases.

Note down the country where a metric differs clearly, and the queries or pages where that difference is concentrated.

How Do You Find Where Your Site's Performance Improved or Declined?

Comparing two countries shows you the difference between them over the same period. To find the countries where your performance improved or declined, compare two date ranges:

  1. Click “More” next to the date ranges at the top of the report to open the “Date range” window, then choose the “Compare” tab.
  2. Select the two periods, such as the last three months versus the three months before them, then click “Apply.”
  3. Open the “Countries” tab, where you'll find each country's numbers for both periods and a column showing the difference between them.
  4. Sort the table by the difference column to see the countries where clicks rose or fell the most.

For a fair comparison, view the data “Weekly” or “Monthly,” as Google recommends, and don't end the period yesterday, because data usually takes two to three days to be complete.

If you notice clicks dropping in a country, examine it on its own: set the country filter to that country only, compare the last complete month with the month before it, then open the “Queries” tab and then “Pages,” and sort each by the difference column. You'll end up with a short list of the queries and pages that changed the most.

If you want to compare one country with the total of your other countries, the comparison feature isn't enough, because it sets one value against another, and Google's help pages don't describe comparing one country with a group of countries. Instead, set up two views for the same period: the first with the country filter on that country, and the second with the country filter on the rest of your countries, and record each view's numbers in a simple table. If you add a comparison between two periods to the second view, make sure the filter bar shows both the country filter and the date comparison; if it doesn't, set the date range under “More” to each period in turn and record its numbers.

If you've only recently started selling in a country, say your store began shipping to Kuwait three months ago, its change between the two periods will look large regardless, because the first period has little or nothing to compare against. Instead, track its performance month by month since launch.

Mistakes That Make Country Comparisons Misleading

  1. Reading the combined average position as your ranking in each country. Google calculates average position across all impressions, so a country with more impressions carries more weight in the combined figure. Hypothetical numbers for illustration: a large country with 9,000 impressions at around position 4 and a small country with 1,000 impressions at around position 12 give a combined figure of about 4.8. Even if the small country drops to position 20, the combined figure won't go above about 5.6. This only illustrates the weighting idea; it isn't the formula Google uses. So look at each country's row separately.
  2. Judging a small country on a handful of numbers. With small numbers, CTR and position fluctuate quickly, so look at them over longer periods and in the “Monthly” view. And if its list of queries is short, that's to be expected, because the report omits very rare searches to protect searchers' privacy.
  3. Comparing specific days across countries. Days in the report are based on Pacific Time, so a report day starts in the morning or around midday in the Gulf countries and Egypt. As a result, a single sale day in your country may be split across two days in the report.
  4. Expecting the numbers to match other analytics tools. Google lists reasons why Search Console data differs from tools such as Google Analytics, including privacy protection, the way data is processed, and time zone differences. Use Search Console to understand search, and your analytics tool to understand what happens on your site.
  5. Mixing up the Search report with other reports. The Discover and Google News reports are separate from the Search report, and in them, country means something different.

How Do You Use Comparison Results to Improve Your Site's Visibility in Each Country?

A comparison is only useful if it leads to a decision. Once you've identified the country, queries and pages where your performance changed, start with what the numbers point to:

  • If impressions dropped in a country, your site is now showing up less in search results there. Start with the pages that lost the most impressions, and make sure they still answer what people in that country are searching for.
  • If impressions held steady but clicks dropped, check your ranking for those queries first. If the ranking hasn't changed and CTR stays low, Google suggests reviewing the page title and description so they describe the page content more accurately.
  • If a new country is growing slowly, look at the queries your site appears for there, and consider whether your pages need content specific to that country or to the way people there search.

Remember that the report shows you where performance changed and what changed, but not why. The cause could be a stronger local competitor, a change you made on your site, or a local season. Google points out that linking a change in performance to an edit you made isn't easy, because other events, such as news or a competitor's site improving, can also play a part. And don't judge a country by searching Google yourself, because results vary by time, location, device and search history.

Make this review a monthly habit: in the first days of each month, once the previous month's data is complete, compare it with the month before, pick one country that needs a closer look, and note down what changed in your business there.

If you see differences between your countries that affect important decisions and the report doesn't explain why, it can help to have a specialist read your data alongside what you know about each market. That's exactly what SEO consulting at SEO House is for.
